entry.title: Revisiting Multi-Agent Scaling
entry.content:
Agent teams must decide how to divide work, share information, and combine their contributions as more agents join. This post reviews seven approaches, asking who coordinates the work and how feedback changes the system, with or without updating model parameters.

Here, training-free means that the LLM weights stay fixed. Prompts, memories, populations, and team structures can still change. With training means that feedback updates model parameters; it does not necessarily mean test-time training on the current task. Decentralized refers to coordination without a central LLM dispatcher. Shared services and common rules can still be present.

01 · Training-free

Frozen models can still change how they work together. A supervisor can reorganize a team, agents can build on shared discoveries, and a population can change through selection. These methods place adaptation in the system around the LLM.

Centralized: a supervisor changes the team

Evolving Agent Teams (EAT) uses a supervisor to inspect progress on program optimization and revise the team’s roles, coordination, and knowledge management. It can isolate a difficult debugging investigation or add a role that synthesizes earlier discoveries. A persistent filesystem carries experience between teams; LLM weights stay fixed.

I find the distinction between improving a program and changing the process used to improve it useful. The appropriate process can change after a bottleneck is removed. EAT provides empirical examples, with few repeated runs and no mathematical guarantee of escaping local optima.

Decentralized: markets, information, and work

These three approaches remove the central LLM dispatcher, but place coordination in different parts of the system.

EoM: economic selection of participants

Economy of Minds: Emerging Multi-Agent Intelligence with Economic Interactions allocates turns through auctions. Eligible agents have fixed bids; the winner pays the preceding actor and receives environment rewards. Wealth influences survival and prompt mutation; bankrupt agents are replaced.

The paper calls this an optimization or training phase, but LLM weights stay fixed. Evaluation freezes the population and disables economic updates.

EoM offers a mechanism for rewarding earlier work through downstream activity. I would distinguish this payment signal from a measurement of causal contribution.

ScaleMAS: selective access to collective knowledge

Scaling Multi-Agent Intelligence with Substrate-Centric Coordination introduces ScaleMAS. Agents publish messages, search by content, and visit messages by address. References link a new message to earlier work; search combines relevance with citation signals to select what a reader sees.

This addresses an information-access problem: a larger group produces more material, but every agent has limited attention. Persistent messages allow discoveries to outlive their authors, while bounded reads limit how much enters a context at once. They do not bound the total cost of running the group.

Matched-inference-budget comparisons show gains. Scaling to 128 agents is demonstrated on Contradiction Audit; other tasks saturate earlier.

Agensh: self-assigned work with shared integration

Agensh: Scaling Organizational Intelligence to 1,024 Agents gives each worker a cooperation loop: gather context, claim a task, act, verify, and merge progress. A Git workspace holds contributions, messages support coordination, and shared context records findings and work intentions.

Workers choose tasks from the evolving state of the project. They can negotiate overlapping claims and resolve merge conflicts without waiting for a central planner. Claims are coordination signals, not a guarantee of exclusive ownership; textual merge checks also cannot establish that the combined program is correct.

Experiments use a six-hour budget, reaching 128 agents across five tasks and 1,024 on Pandoc. Equal-cost efficiency requires a separate comparison.

The distinction between ScaleMAS and Agensh matters: retrieving a useful finding and integrating a verified code change solve different problems. My reading is that their mechanisms could complement each other. Better information selection could help a worker decide what to claim and how to execute it, but that combination needs its own evaluation.

02 · With training

When coordination decisions are generated by a model, feedback can also change the probability of making those decisions again. MPT, Avalon-M1 and s³ differ in who organizes work and how a team outcome becomes a learning signal.

MPT: learn how to act and when to participate

Learning Self-Orchestration in Decentralized Agent Swarms introduces market-based post-training. Bids both select an actor and determine how credit passes backward. Counterfactual continuations teach participation: preference learning favors the bid associated with the better outcome. Action and participation then adapt together.

Experiments start with complementary roles and require restorable environments. They support learned turn allocation; arbitrary role discovery and coordination among hundreds of simultaneous workers remain further questions.

Avalon-M1: reinforce useful parallel work

Avalon-M1: Reinforcement Learning from Collective Rewards trains a shared policy used by a CEO and specialist agents. RLCR applies one collective advantage across the agents’ generated tokens, without explicitly estimating each member’s contribution. The CEO and workers are trained jointly.

How to Train a Swarm explains how the training setup rewards useful parallel work. Avalon-M1 caps wall-clock time and scores progress at the deadline, using environments with measurable intermediate returns. The cap grows during training. Equal returns before the deadline receive equal scores, so this is not a reward for every second saved.

Channels, direct messages and an archive let agents divide work and reuse discoveries. Communication consumes time, so additional messages alone do not establish better coordination. Useful comparisons measure task progress at matched elapsed time and matched token budgets. The report’s latency comparisons use derived latency.

RLCR’s flat advantage remains a coarse signal over long episodes. The initial CEO-plus-specialist setup trains teams of at most nine agents; generalization to much larger collectives remains open.

s³: Simple Scaling of Swarms via Cooperative Multi-agent RL

Agents share a policy but keep private histories. They choose when to work, send messages and read replies, without assigned roles or a central dispatcher. Team success means at least one agent answers correctly; successful teams pay a normalized token cost.

Eight independent team attempts on the same problem supply the reward group:

\[A_g=\frac{R_g-\bar R}{\sigma_R+\epsilon}.\]

Every generated token in team $g$ receives $A_g$. The loss averages within teams, then across teams. Information aggregation uses Qwen3-0.6B; exploration uses Qwen3-1.7B. Training uses four agents, with evaluation up to sixteen. Matched-budget controls show gains from learned communication in these tasks, including less duplicate exploration. Scaling to arbitrary swarm sizes remains untested.

What I would compare

MPT spends extra rollouts on participation credit. Avalon-M1 and s³ use shared outcomes, with different assumptions about organization. Their environments and budgets differ, so reported scores do not provide a direct ranking.

Comparing three training designs
Design choiceMPTAvalon-M1 / RLCRs³
ParticipationLearned bids select the next actor.A trained CEO delegates work.No fixed roles or turn order.
FeedbackLocal credit and counterfactual preferences.Shared collective advantage.Team-relative advantage.
ParametersSeparate across agents.Shared across the team.Shared across the team.
Cost to examineAdditional branching rollouts.Learning from a coarse signal over long episodes.Messaging and inference contention.

For a controlled comparison, I would hold the backbone, task interface, and available tools fixed, then measure performance against both training compute and deployment cost. Extra rollouts for contribution estimates belong in the training budget. At deployment, quality at a fixed elapsed time and quality at a fixed inference budget answer different questions. An improvement in one does not establish an improvement in the other.

I would also separate three decisions that often get grouped under “coordination”: which information to read, which work to undertake, and how to distribute feedback for learning. A system may handle one well while struggling with another. That suggests useful combinations to test, such as selective retrieval inside a self-assigned work loop, or learning a supervisor from records of successful team reorganizations. These are research directions, rather than results established by the papers above.

Paper links and versions used
  1. Evolving Agent Teams · v1, October 2026.
  2. Economy of Minds: Emerging Multi-Agent Intelligence with Economic Interactions · v2, October 2026.
  3. Scaling Multi-Agent Intelligence with Substrate-Centric Coordination · v1, October 2026.
  4. Agensh: Scaling Organizational Intelligence to 1,024 Agents · v1, September 2026.
  5. Learning Self-Orchestration in Decentralized Agent Swarms · v2, October 2026.
  6. Avalon-M1: Reinforcement Learning from Collective Rewards · October 2026 report; How to Train a Swarm, November 2, 2026.
  7. s³: Simple Scaling of Swarms via Cooperative Multi-agent RL · v1, November 5, 2026.

entry.title: Revisiting Self-Improving Agents for Autoresearch
entry.content:
Research agents propose solutions, evaluate them, and use the results to decide what to try next. This post reviews how methods manage search history, generate candidates, and learn research decisions to make better use of a limited evaluation budget.

Methods

SwarmEvolve: Latent Agent Swarms for Evolutionary Discovery and Optimization

SwarmEvolve changes how candidate programs are proposed. Each round runs 10 swarms of 45 agents for 40 latent steps. Within each swarm, a novelty filter retains 30 diverse trajectories. A summarizer reads their KV caches and writes one program; evaluation then updates the archive. Diversity is measured in hidden-state space, not guaranteed at the level of program behavior.

The LLM weights stay fixed. Unlike parameter training, the loop improves programs and the search archive. Experiments cover 21 discovery and scientific-computing tasks, using Qwen3 8B, 14B and 32B-FP8 for 60 minutes on one GPU. Reported speedups concern this search setup; they do not make arbitrary evaluators cheaper.

Takeaways

Research agents can improve through context management, cheaper proposal generation, or training the roles that decide what to investigate. The comparison below focuses on context and learned decisions; SwarmEvolve adds a way to explore more proposals per unit of compute.

What’s the Next Step?

I see evaluation time as a major constraint on self-improving research agents. A promising idea still needs to be tested, and those tests can dominate the research budget. In DuoDiscover’s vLLM study, one full evaluation takes about 85 minutes. This points to two directions.

Use fewer evaluations

How can we find a better solution with fewer calls to the evaluator? Training-free methods can use past results to select more informative experiments and avoid repeating failed attempts. With training, a research policy can learn which directions are worth pursuing. Both aim for sample-efficient search: reaching a stronger verified result within a fixed evaluation budget.

Memento 3 offers a training-free example. The agent turns interaction feedback into a revisable handbook of environment rules, then compiles those rules into an executable world model. It checks the model against past observations and uses it to plan future actions. The LLM stays frozen; the handbook and simulator improve as evidence accumulates. This illustrates an algorithmic route to fewer real interactions: use what the agent has learned to guide its next attempt.

Make evaluations cheaper

Can a cheap approximation tell us which candidates deserve a full evaluation? Smaller test suites, shorter runs or surrogate models could make it possible to explore more candidates with the same resources.

DuoDiscover offers an example: agents develop optimization targets together with cheap, tailored proxy evaluators. They search using these proxies, then confirm improvements with the full evaluator. Fidelity tests also check whether proxy rankings still agree with full evaluations as the search progresses.

Working on self-improving agents, I’m always interested in the models people choose and the tasks they test them on. Some familiar tasks, such as Erdős problems and packing benchmarks, already seem close to saturation. I’ve collected the models and tasks from these papers below as a reference for planning new experiments.

  • Models — model choices, agent setups and evaluation budgets.
  • Tasks — benchmarks, evaluation time, resources and recent progress.
entry.summary: How research agents use evaluation feedback to improve solutions within a fixed budget.

entry.title: Revisiting RL for LLM Post-Training
entry.content:
Policy-gradient methods turn rollout feedback into model updates, with different choices about how to estimate advantages and control update size. This post reviews PPO and related methods through five perspectives on learning efficiency, the role of critics, and update stability.

Need a refresher on PPO? Start with the basics.

01Learning without value networksFlashREINFORCE · SPO · CoPE↗ 02Changing what critics doTEMPO · AC2 · SAPO↗ 03Changing what critics seeBPCO · LVRL · Agentic judging · Post-Thinking↗ 04Stabilizing policy updatesSAO · Score Centering · REINFORCE Zero · EasyPPO · StableReinforce↗ 05To Critic or Not to CriticBatch size · bootstrapping · task horizon↗

Learning without value networks

FlashREINFORCE and SPO use statistical baselines; CoPE adds action forecasting to GRPO. All three learn without a value network.

FlashREINFORCE

  • No learned critic: For a batch of $B$ independent prompts, center the observed rewards:

    \[\bar R=\frac{1}{B}\sum_{j=1}^{B}R_j, \qquad A_i=R_i-\bar R.\]

    A response above the batch mean receives positive advantage; one below it receives negative advantage.

  • Trajectory filtering: Weight token updates by current-to-rollout probability ratios. For each sampled token, let $p_t$ and $q_t$ be its rollout and current-policy probabilities at the same history:

    \[\begin{aligned} d_t &= p_t\log\frac{p_t}{q_t}+(1-p_t)\log\frac{1-p_t}{1-q_t},\\ \bar D &= \frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}d_t,\qquad m=\mathbf{1}[\bar D\leq\delta]. \end{aligned}\]

    Keep the whole trajectory only when $m=1$; $T$ counts model-generated tokens and $\delta$ is the threshold. This Bernoulli KL is a lower-bound proxy for full-vocabulary KL. Details.

  • Equal trajectory weight: For token losses $\ell_{i,t}$ that include advantage and importance weighting, aggregate as

    \[L=\frac{1}{B}\sum_{i=1}^{B}m_i \left(\frac{1}{T_i}\sum_{t=1}^{T_i}\ell_{i,t}\right).\]

    Here $m_i$ is the trajectory gate above. Averaging within each response removes its explicit length multiplier. Each fresh batch receives one update.

SPO

  • Persistent baseline: For prompt $x$, compare reward $R$ with the tracker’s estimate before this rollout:

    \[A=R-\hat v_{\mathrm{old}}(x), \qquad \tilde A=\frac{A-\bar A_{\mathcal B}}{\sigma_{A,\mathcal B}}.\]

    The baseline uses past outcomes; normalization uses the current batch $\mathcal B$ across prompts.

  • Adaptive memory: The Bayesian tracker has an equivalent moving-average update:

    \[\hat v_{\mathrm{new}}(x)=\hat v_{\mathrm{old}}(x) +\eta_x\bigl(R-\hat v_{\mathrm{old}}(x)\bigr).\]

    The step size $\eta_x$ reflects policy change and accumulated evidence. A larger policy shift discounts older evidence more strongly. The tracker also supports prioritized prompt sampling.

CoPE

  • Forecast successful actions: From history $h_t$, predict the recorded action chunk $a_{t:t+K}$. For the successful subset $\mathcal S_x$ of a rollout group:

    \[L_{\mathrm{AF},x}= -\frac{\displaystyle\sum_{\tau\in\mathcal S_x}\sum_t \log p_\theta(a_{t:t+K}\mid h_t)} {\max(1,|\mathcal S_x|)}.\]

    This averages supervision over successful trajectories; a group with no success contributes zero forecasting loss.

  • Shared policy backbone: Minimize

    \[L=L_{\mathrm{GRPO}}+\eta\,\mathbb E_x[L_{\mathrm{AF},x}].\]

    The coefficient $\eta$ controls the extra supervision. Acting and forecasting use the same weights with different instructions; inference still takes one action at a time.

Changing what critics do

Change how policy and value learning share a model, or use values to learn before a long rollout finishes.

TEMPO — dots

Test-Time-Scaled Value Estimation with Macro-Step Policy Optimization, from Xiaohongshu’s dots team.

  • Macro-step returns: Resume saved states for $H$ interactions. In undiscounted notation, branch $i$ supplies

    \[G_i=\sum_{h=0}^{H-1}r_{i,h}+\hat V(s_{i,H}), \qquad y(s)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}G_i.\]

    Terminal states have zero remaining value. $G_i$ trains the actor; $y(s)$ targets the starting-state value.

  • Generative critic: Reason over history, optionally using tools and privileged environment information. Call it at segment boundaries to limit cost.

  • Learn to evaluate: Warm up with complete-trajectory returns, then use TD targets. Reward critic estimates by normalized accuracy and center rewards within each state’s group. Actor and critic share parameters and use GRPO, with different prompts and rewards.

The appendix derives importance correction for reused prefixes; segment updates alone do not remove policy staleness.

AC2

  • Short continuations: From replayed prefix $s$, sample chunks $c_i$. Once the problem passes critic-readiness checks, unfinished chunks can use predicted endpoint values:

    \[v_i=\begin{cases} R_i, & \text{complete response},\\ V_\theta(s\cdot c_i), & \text{unfinished chunk}. \end{cases}\]

    The symbol $\cdot$ means concatenation. A trusted prediction can replace the cost of completing a response.

  • Chunk advantages: Compare $G$ continuations of the same prefix:

    \[\bar v=\frac{1}{G}\sum_{j=1}^{G}v_j, \qquad \hat A_i=v_i-\bar v.\]

    All new tokens in chunk $c_i$ share $\hat A_i$. Train the shared generative critic at $s$ to output the rounded group mean $\bar v$ as a value token; replayed prefix tokens receive no actor loss.

  • Full-rollout audits: Complete a fraction of ready problems to check critic predictions against actual outcomes.

SAPO

Single-Rollout Autoregressive Policy Optimization. Code.

  • Shared logit readouts: Reuse two reserved vocabulary logits to estimate values from the policy model:

    \[\begin{aligned} v_\theta(c)&=\frac{z_{\theta,+}(c)-z_{\theta,-}(c)}{\tau_v},\\ V_\theta(s_t)&=R_{\max}v_\theta(s_t),\\ Q_\theta(s_t,a_t)&=R_{\max}v_\theta([s_t;a_t]). \end{aligned}\]

    The pre-response readout cannot see the current action; the post-response readout cannot see the next observation. These are unbounded scalar estimates, not generated value answers. The reserved entries are excluded from action sampling.

  • Turn-level credit: Collect one trajectory per task. Compute GAE across interaction turns using $V$, standardize across batch turns, then broadcast each turn’s advantage to its response tokens. PPO ratios and clipping remain token-level; no same-task rollout group is needed.

  • Auxiliary Q learning: Fit scaled targets with clipped value regression alongside the policy objective:

    \[\begin{aligned} y_t^V&=V_t^{\mathrm{old}}+A_t^{\mathrm{turn}},\\ y_t^Q&=r_t+\gamma(1-d_t)Q_{t+1}^{\mathrm{old}}. \end{aligned}\]

    $Q_{t+1}^{\mathrm{old}}$ evaluates the next action from that same rollout; $d_t$ marks termination. The SARSA target trains the shared value representation. $Q$ does not directly enter GAE.

Changing what critics see

Give evaluators more evidence: reference answers, completed traces, tool checks, or the model’s own response. The methods below use that evidence for value estimation, credit assignment, or self-judging; these are different learning signals.

BPCO

  • Ground the critic: With outcome-only rewards and no discounting, use

    \[R_{\min}\leq V_\phi(s_t)\leq R_{\max}, \qquad L_V=\mathbb E[(V_\phi(s_t)-R)^2].\]

    Bound the value head and fit observed final rewards, avoiding targets built from the critic’s own predictions. Optional reference answers or rubrics enter only the critic.

  • Preserve the learning signal: For a response of length $L$, use

    \[\lambda_\pi(L)=1-\frac{1}{\alpha L}, \qquad \lambda_V=1.\]

    Here $\alpha>0$ controls GAE decay. Longer responses use slower decay, preserving distant outcome feedback. Keep raw GAE advantages instead of dividing by the batch standard deviation.

  • Divergence PPO: If $p_t$ is the sampled token’s rollout probability, replace the fixed ratio-clipping interval with

    \[\left[1-\frac{\epsilon}{p_t},\;1+\frac{\epsilon}{p_t}\right].\]

    Its boundaries correspond to an absolute probability change of $\epsilon$. Clipping limits the incentive to move farther, rather than enforcing a hard constraint.

LVRL

  • Frozen LLM critic: Read the completed trajectory, its outcome, and related rollouts to estimate intermediate values $\tilde V_t$. These are hindsight assessments, not prefix-only predictions; no critic training is needed.

  • Anchored credit: For group mean reward $\bar R_G$ and trajectory reward $R$, fix the endpoints and take differences:

    \[\begin{aligned} \tilde V_0&=\bar R_G,\qquad \tilde V_T=R,\\ \bar A_t&=\tilde V_{t+1}-\tilde V_t,\\ \sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\bar A_t&=R-\bar R_G. \end{aligned}\]

    Actual outcomes fix the total credit; the LLM decides its distribution across actions. Divide $\bar A_t$ by the group-wide step standard deviation for training. All tokens in one action share its advantage; anchoring does not guarantee correct local attribution.

Honey I judged the rollouts

Chinmay Karkar’s experiment gives an agentic judge the full trace, verifier verdict and reference answer, with a worked solution when available. It checks calculations and labels spans, adding bounded credit to the outcome advantage:

\[\widetilde A_{i,t}=A_i+\lambda c_{i,t}, \qquad \frac{1}{T_i}\sum_t|\lambda c_{i,t}|\le 0.25.\]

Here $c_{i,t}$ is span credit and $\lambda$ controls its strength, not GAE decay. Unlike LVRL’s anchored value differences, this is an additive adjustment.

The study uses Qwen3.5-4B, rank-16 LoRA, 875 training prompts and 100 held-out prompts, with a 32K response cap. Three 40-step runs compare outcome-only training with $\lambda=0.25$ and $1.0$, using gpt-6-luna as judge. Benchmark differences were near noise; traces mainly showed earlier commitment to answers. This short experiment does not establish an accuracy gain from finer credit.

Self-Improving Post-Thinking

The model generates an answer, then a post-thought that judges that answer. This teaches evaluation after generation rather than estimating a partial trajectory’s future return.

With a strong teacher, post-thoughts receive supervised targets alongside answer optimization. With verifiable answers, the model can learn both roles through RL:

\[\begin{aligned} R_{\mathrm{answer}}&=\mathbf 1[\text{answer correct}],\\ R_{\mathrm{judge}}&=\mathbf 1[\text{verdict matches correctness}]. \end{aligned}\]

This schematic omits the malformed-verdict penalty. A correct judgment of a wrong answer can receive positive judging reward. Teacher supervision or a verifier supplies the check; the model’s own verdict is not treated as ground truth. At inference, judgments can help select candidates or decide when to abstain. The reported applications cover safety, reasoning and confidence calibration.

Stabilizing policy updates

Control errors from asynchronous sampling, mismatched probabilities, and noisy critic training.

SAO

  • Single-rollout sampling: Collect one trajectory per prompt asynchronously. A learned critic supplies the baseline, so training need not wait for sibling rollouts.

  • Token masking: Let $\mu$ be the logged rollout policy and $\pi_\theta$ the learner:

    \[\begin{aligned} \rho_t&=\frac{\pi_\theta(a_t\mid s_t)}{\mu(a_t\mid s_t)},\\ w_t&=\rho_t\,\mathbf 1[1-\epsilon_\ell<\rho_t<1+\epsilon_h]. \end{aligned}\]

    Use $w_t$ to weight the token’s advantage-gradient contribution. Outside the interval its contribution is zero, regardless of advantage sign.

  • Skip-observation GAE: Let $t^+$ index the next model-generated token, skipping intervening observation tokens:

    \[\begin{aligned} \delta_t&=r_t+\gamma V(s_{t^+})-V(s_t),\\ \hat A_t&=\delta_t+\gamma\lambda\hat A_{t^+}. \end{aligned}\]

    The next state still includes tool feedback in its context. GAE simply does not recurse through each tool-output token; terminal continuation values are zero.

  • Critic updates: Warm up the critic, freeze its attention layers, and update it twice per actor update to help it track the changing policy.

Score Centering

  • Why center the score? At a fixed prefix $s$, let $p_a=\pi_\theta(a\mid s)$ be the learner, $q_a=\mu(a\mid s)$ the sampler, and $\psi_a=\nabla_\theta\log p_a$ the score. Write $A=\hat A(s,a)$ for the advantage, held fixed during the actor update. Kunhao Zheng’s decomposition makes the unwanted drift explicit:

    \[\mathbb E_q[A\psi] =\underbrace{\operatorname{Cov}_q(A,\psi)}_{\text{signal}} +\underbrace{\mathbb E_q[A]\,\mathbb E_q[\psi]}_{\text{drift}}.\]

    On-policy, $\mathbb E_p[\psi]=0$. When sampling and training distributions differ, that identity need not hold under $q$: even adding a constant to every advantage can change the expected update.

  • Remove that drift: Subtract the sampler’s expected score:

    \[\begin{aligned} c(s)&=\sum_a q_a\psi_a,\\ g_{\mathrm{SC}}(s)&=\mathbb E_q\!\left[A\bigl(\psi-c(s)\bigr)\right] =\operatorname{Cov}_q(A,\psi). \end{aligned}\]

    Centering advantages by their exact mean at this prefix would zero the first factor of the drift term; score centering zeros the second. A batch-wide zero mean does not guarantee a zero mean at every prefix. The remaining covariance is still under $q$, so this is not a complete off-policy correction.

  • Practical correction: Store sampler probabilities for its top-$k$ tokens $H$ and approximate the remaining mass using the trainer’s distribution:

    \[\begin{aligned} \rho&=\frac{1-\sum_{a\in H}q_a}{1-\sum_{a\in H}p_a},\\ \hat c(s)&=\sum_{a\in H}(q_a-\rho p_a)\psi_a. \end{aligned}\]

    This assigns unlogged tokens probability $\hat q_a=\rho p_a$ and uses $\sum_a p_a\psi_a=0$ to avoid summing over the tail. Hold the correction coefficients fixed when differentiating the loss.

  • IS + score centering: With importance weight $w_a=f(p_a/q_a)$,

    \[g_{\mathrm{IS+SC}}(s) =\mathbb E_{a\sim q}\!\left[ A_a\left( \underbrace{w_a\psi_a}_{\mathrm{IS}} -\underbrace{\sum_b q_b w_b\psi_b}_{\mathrm{score\ centering}} \right)\right].\]

    IS reweights the sampled score; centering subtracts its mean under the sampler. For exact, unclipped IS ($w_a=p_a/q_a$), the centering term is zero.

A feedback-loop view

Cameron Wolfe’s illustrated explanation connects mismatch to repeated updates: the trainer moves, the sampler refreshes, and mismatch can affect the next update again. Small discrepancies can therefore accumulate. The paper’s experiments distinguish quantization from policy staleness; score centering and importance sampling can be useful together. Centering removes the sampler-mean score, rather than centering rewards again.

The same correction in logit space

Qiuyang Mang’s discussion suggests examining logits directly. The following derivation makes that view explicit for unweighted, full-vocabulary score centering at a fixed prefix. Let $p=\operatorname{softmax}(z)$, let $q$ be the detached sampler distribution, and let $e_a$ select token $a$:

\[\begin{aligned} \nabla_z\log p_a&=e_a-p,\\ \mathbb E_{a\sim q}[\nabla_z\log p_a]&=q-p,\\ (e_a-p)-(q-p)&=e_a-q. \end{aligned}\]

The centered contribution is $A_a(e_a-q)$. If all actions have the same advantage, its expectation under $q$ is zero; the uncentered contribution retains $A(q-p)$. The cancellation is local to this prefix. In parameter space, the logit Jacobian still matters; importance weighting, masking and top-$k$ approximations change the expression.

REINFORCE Zero

REINFORCE Zero: Kernel Alignment Unlocks Stable Asynchronous RL with Importance Sampling separates two sources of rollout–learner mismatch. Asynchronous rollouts use older weights. Numerical execution can also change token probabilities at identical weights and histories. Here, kernels are GPU computation kernels.

  • Align execution: Trainer–inference invariance (TII) matches rollout and learner probabilities using batch-invariant kernels and matched operators. This removes the numerical component of mismatch.
  • Correct policy lag: Use the full token-level importance ratio, with the actual recorded sampling probability in the denominator. There is no PPO ratio clipping or token/sequence rejection gate.

The algorithm uses group-mean advantages and no learned critic:

\[A_i=R_i-\frac{1}{G}\sum_{j\in\mathcal G(i)}R_j, \qquad \widehat L(\theta)=-\frac{1}{B}\sum_{i=1}^{B}\frac{1}{T_i} \sum_{t=1}^{T_i}A_i\frac{\pi_\theta(a_{it}\mid h_{it})}{\mu_i(a_{it}\mid h_{it})}.\]

Here $\mathcal G(i)$ contains the $G$ responses to the same prompt, $B$ is the batch size, and $T_i$ counts generated action tokens. Tool observations do not contribute to the loss. Differentiate the numerator while holding advantages and recorded behavior probabilities fixed. Unlike FlashREINFORCE’s batch-wide baseline, this baseline uses multiple responses per prompt.

Why align kernels if importance sampling already corrects the update? A correct mean does not control variance. Rare actions with large importance weights can produce large updates. The paper’s Gaussian model shows that mismatch can make expected squared error grow even as the mean parameter approaches the optimum. At a fixed history, full IS recovers the target conditional update; Score Centering alone retains the covariance under the sampling policy. Token-level IS does not correct the distribution of entire histories.

The paper reports stable training through 20,000 updates on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B at nominal lags 2 and 8. On 16 GPUs, 12,000 updates take 68.55 hours versus 164.77 for synchronous TII, excluding evaluation: 2.40× training-step throughput, with comparable reasoning quality. This measures wall-clock efficiency, not a 2.40× reduction in samples. The results support unclipped IS under aligned execution; they do not establish that clipping is unnecessary for every PPO workload.

EasyPPO

  • Actor-only truncation filtering: Let $C_i=1$ if response $i$ finishes within the length limit. Apply $C_i$ only to actor loss; keep every rollout in critic training. The critic then learns $\mathbb E[R\mid s]$, rather than $\mathbb E[R\mid s,C=1]$.

  • Noise-weighted critic loss: Let $\hat\sigma_x$ be the return standard deviation across rollouts of prompt $x$:

    \[\begin{aligned} w_x&\propto\frac{1}{\max(\hat\sigma_x,\varepsilon)},\\ L_V&=\mathbb E_{x,i,t}\!\left[w_x\bigl(V_\phi(s_{i,t})-R_i\bigr)^2\right]. \end{aligned}\]

    High-variance prompts receive less weight, even when their mean reward is the same. This changes their influence on training, not their reward targets; $\varepsilon$ prevents division by zero.

  • Smaller critic minibatches: Clip each minibatch gradient $g$ separately:

    \[g_{\mathrm{clip}}=g\min\!\left(1,\frac{c}{\lVert g\rVert}\right).\]

    The threshold $c$ limits gradient norm. Smaller minibatches restrict how many other samples an outlier can suppress through this shared rescaling. The actor retains the PPO objective.

StableReinforce

Martin Marek’s October 25 thread identifies StableReinforce as REINFORCE with Monte Carlo score centering. His custom loss reproduces its gradients within numerical precision in a controlled probe. This is independent reverse-engineering evidence; Tinker has not published the full policy-gradient formula.

  • Estimate the mean score by sampling: Marek infers eight auxiliary next-token draws at each prefix:

    \[\begin{aligned} u_k&\sim q(\cdot\mid s),\qquad K=8,\\ \hat c(s)&=\frac1K\sum_{k=1}^{K}\nabla_\theta\log p_\theta(u_k\mid s),\\ \hat g_{\mathrm{SC}}&=A\left[\nabla_\theta\log p_\theta(a\mid s)-\hat c(s)\right]. \end{aligned}\]

    With independent sampler draws, $\hat c$ is an unbiased estimate of $c(s)$. This trades the original paper’s deterministic top-$k$ approximation for Monte Carlo noise; it does not make the whole update an unbiased on-policy gradient.

  • Why the gradient gives it away: For logits $z$ and a one-hot token vector $e_a$, $\nabla_z\log p(a)=e_a-p$. Subtracting the sampled mean cancels the dense $-p$ term:

    \[\nabla_z\log p(a)-\frac1K\sum_k\nabla_z\log p(u_k) =e_a-\frac1K\sum_k e_{u_k}.\]

    Only the selected tokens remain. Marek observes this sparse pattern in StableReinforce, then matches gradients across all layers with a custom centered loss. The cancellation describes the policy-gradient term; a separate KL penalty can add a dense gradient.

How did he recover the gradients?

The probe uses Qwen3.5-4B with rank-1 LoRA. An Adam step with $\varepsilon=10{,}000$ makes the denominator nearly constant, so weight changes reveal the gradient up to a scale. The rank-1 output adapter then exposes the logit-gradient direction. In the single-token probe, StableReinforce moves only eight logit coordinates, with corrections in multiples of $1/8$; ordinary REINFORCE produces a dense gradient. Probe setup · gradient match.

  • Official API and KL: Tinker accepts caller-supplied advantages and records sampling information for stability. Its default, optional $k_1$ regularizer is

    \[L_{\mathrm{KL}}=\beta\sum_t\left[\log q(a_t\mid s_t)-\log p_\theta(a_t\mid s_t)\right].\]

    This estimates $\beta\,\mathrm{KL}(q|p_\theta)$ at sampled prefixes, pulling the learner toward the sampler rather than a frozen reference model. The documentation also offers a $k_3$ estimator. Score centering changes the reward-weighted update; KL separately limits divergence.

To Critic or Not to Critic

To Critic Or Not To Critic compares PPO and GRPO under a shared actor objective, varying trajectory batch size, critic reliance and task horizon. Across more than 1,200 runs, including 96 LLM runs, a critic generally helps most at small batches. Larger batches let GRPO catch up, especially when PPO bootstraps heavily from imperfect values.

The authors’ analysis separates expected-gradient alignment $c$ from gradient noise scale $\nu$:

\[\mathbb E[\cos(\hat g_B,g)]\approx\frac{c}{\sqrt{1+\nu/B}}.\]

Here $g$ is the true policy gradient and $\hat g_B$ is its batch estimate. Increasing $B$ reduces noise; it does not remove directional bias. Smaller GAE $\lambda$ relies more on the critic. Longer or more complex tasks generally require larger batches before GRPO catches up.

Regime What the study finds
Small batch / limited compute Critic variance reduction can offset its training cost.
Larger batch Sampling reduces noise; critic bias and overhead remain.
Longer horizon The crossover shifts toward larger batches.

LLM experiments use Qwen2.5-3B Base on DeepScaleR and Qwen3.5-4B on TMax-15K terminal tasks. Math uses three seeds; terminal training uses one. Reported compute includes rollout and actor–critic costs, estimated in H100 GPU-hours. These are conditional comparisons, not a universal batch-size threshold or a ranking of every critic method above.
